query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A covariance‐based entropy evaluation method—one that uses short-run ab initio simulations (or Monte Carlo sampling) to compute the covariance matrix of atomic displacements and thereby extract vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions—can be used to estimate the free energies of both solid and fluid phases near the fusion point with accuracy comparable to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics/TOR-TILD approaches while reducing computational cost substantially.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental or binary systems (and by extension selected multicomponent high-entropy alloys) in their high-temperature (fusion) regime, where both solid and fluid phases are characterized by full vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions.
generation.intervention: Replace costly, long-timescale explicit ab initio MD simulations with a protocol that performs short simulations or Monte Carlo sampling to compute the covariance matrix of atomic displacements. This statistical sampling then yields an effective vibrational density of states and thus the full vibrational (and some anharmonic) entropy contributions for both phases.
generation.conditions: Simulations are performed at high temperatures near the fusion transition. Controlled variables include cell size (sufficient for representative sampling), short simulation times (with thorough averaging over symmetry operations), and by using existing experimental lattice parameters when needed. The procedure is evaluated using the same composition and thermal boundaries as in traditional AIMD and TOR-TILD studies.
generation.structural_mediator: The covariance matrix of atomic displacements, which encapsulates the vibrational modes and local correlations that govern the entropy.
generation.mechanism: By statistically sampling atomic displacements from relatively short trajectories and exploiting inherent symmetry, the method reconstructs the vibrational density of states as well as anharmonic effects (and indirectly electron–vibration coupling). These features, normally derived from much longer MD simulations, allow for a faithful estimation of free energies while significantly reducing computation time.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method will yield free energy estimates (and derived fusion properties) that are accurate—that is, within acceptable margins of the explicit ab initio MD/TOR-TILD baseline—and will potentially reduce computational cost by an order of magnitude or more.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD methods that compute free energies via long, direct simulations retaining full vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration coupling effects.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be most reliable for elemental and binary systems and may extend to multicomponent high-entropy systems within high-temperature regimes near fusion. Its performance is contingent on the validity of the Gaussian (or similar) approximation for the atomic displacement distribution.
generation.uncertainty: The degree to which the covariance-based method can capture all anharmonic effects and electron–vibration coupling exactly in multicomponent or extremely anharmonic fluid phases remains uncertain. The exact speedup factor and fidelity in those realms need further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a side-by-side comparison for a representative material near its fusion temperature. Compute the free energies (and derived observables such as fusion temperature) using both the traditional long-run explicit ab initio MD/TOR-TILD approach and the new short-run covariance-based method.
measurements: Free energy values for solid and liquid phases
Vibrational entropy and other entropy contributions
Fusion temperature (or other derived phase-transition properties)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the free energies or derived fusion observables computed with the covariance-based method deviate beyond the acceptable experimental or computational uncertainty (i.e. do not match the baseline results within predefined error margins), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe vibrational entropy of a solid at finite temperature is investigated from the perspective of information theory. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations generate ensembles of atomic configurations at finite temperature from which we obtain the N-body distribution of atomic displacements, ρN. We calculate the information-theoretic entropy from the expectation value of lnρN. At a first level of approximation, treating individual atomic displacements independently, our method may be applied using Debye–Waller B-factors, allowing diffraction experiments to obtain an upper bound on the thermodynamic entropy. At the next level of approximation we correct the overestimation through inclusion of displacement covariances. We apply this approach to elemental body-centered cubic sodium and face-centered cubic aluminum, showing good agreement with experimental values above the Debye temperatures of the metals. Below the Debye temperatures, we extract an effective vibrational density of states from eigenvalues of the covariance matrix, and then evaluate the entropy quantum mechanically, again yielding good agreement with experiment down to low temperatures. This quantum model is harmonic in the sense that it is exact for quadratic potentials U, but it incorporates anharmonicity through the effective vibrational frequencies which were derived from the simulated covariance matrix. Errors due to applying the quantum harmonic model should be small at low temperatures, where motion generically becomes harmonic. Some prior studies employ time-dependent velocity correlation functions, then Fourier transform over time to obtain frequencies [,,]. The systematics of that approach differ markedly from ours, as in principle we do not require time evolution at all; we only simulate trajectories for the sake of enlarging our configurational ensemble. The model Hamiltonian can be constructed in the actual harmonic limit of small oscillations by evaluating the force constants within density functional perturbation theory. This mode substantially underestimates the high temperature entropy as it neglects thermal expansion. The quasiharmonic approximation can be used to predict thermal expansion, resulting in improved agreement, or better yet we can evaluate the force constants at the experimental lattice parameters.
